items.title: Drill: marks and guesses
items.prose: Eight items. Target: about 10 seconds each, 80 seconds in all. Use your own watch; the page has no clock.
items.question: Fill in each answer.

byKey.r7c1: Two left: right half the time, wrong half the time.

explain.text: The 16 blind guesses cost 8 marks on average, so blanks would have scored 51.2. Under a −1/3 rule a guess among three earns $\tfrac19$. Read the rule, then do the sum.

items.question: Type the letter for each row.

A 7 or more heads in 10 flips; B a total of 7 with two dice
A exactly 3 heads in 10; B exactly 7 heads in 10
A a double six at least once in 36 rolls; B a six at least once in 6 rolls
A a normal value over one sd above its mean; B a total of 7
A two cards of the same suit; B exactly 5 heads in 10

feedback.correct: All six. Note your time against 3 minutes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows, computing only the close pairs.

byKey.r2c1: 3 heads is 7 tails: the same count, 120.
byKey.r3c1: Both have $np = 1$; fewer tries at a bigger chance win: 0.665 against 0.637.
byKey.r4c1: One sd up leaves 16% above: 0.159, just under $\tfrac16$.

explain.text: All six pairs were within 0.03 of each other, so benchmarks only got you close. The tie was free by symmetry. The other five needed one line of working each.

items.title: Drill: probability, four options
items.prose: The lesson’s six, now with four options each. The wrong ones are the classic slips: with replacement, the complement, the wrong count. Target: 12 minutes. Use your own watch.
items.question: Type the letter for each row.

At least one head in four flips   **A** 1/16 · **B** 1/2 · **C** 15/16 · **D** 2
Expected rolls of a die up to and including the first 6   **A** 6 · **B** 3.5 · **C** 5 · **D** 1/6
Two people born on the same day of the week   **A** 1/49 · **B** 6/7 · **C** 2/7 · **D** 1/7
Two cards from a deck form a pair   **A** 1/13 · **B** 1/17 · **C** 1/221 · **D** 3/52
Three flips all land the same way   **A** 1/8 · **B** 3/4 · **C** 1/4 · **D** 1/2

feedback.correct: All six. Note your time against 12 minutes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the amber rows from the sample space.

byKey.r0c1: 15 cells of 36: $\tfrac{5}{12}$, B. A treats every total as equally likely; C is the complement.
byKey.r1c1: $1 - \tfrac{1}{16} = \tfrac{15}{16}$, C. A is the complement; D is above 1, so it goes at once.
byKey.r2c1: A chance of $\tfrac16$ a roll takes 6 rolls on average, A. 3.5 is the mean face; 5 counts only the rolls before the 6.
byKey.r3c1: The second person matches the first’s day: $\tfrac17$, D. A names one day for both.
byKey.r4c1: 3 of 51 match: $\tfrac{1}{17}$, B. A forgets the first card left the deck.
byKey.r5c1: HHH or TTT: $\tfrac14$, C. A counts only HHH.

explain.text: Each wrong option matched one slip you know. Crossing out the impossible 2 took no working. Writing the sample space first beats reading the options first.

items.title: Generate a battery section
items.prose:
`battery_generator(seed, mix)` returns `mix[kind]` items of each kind from `random.Random(seed)`, as dicts with `kind`, `text`, four `options` and the `answer`. The three wrong options are near misses: one **reverse operation**, one **misplaced point** and one **slipped digit**. All four options are positive and different.

| Kind | Text | Reverse |
|---|---|---|
| `add` | `634 + 524` | $\lvert a - b\rvert$ |
| `sub` | `972 − 755` | $a + b$ |
| `mul` | `12 × 20` | $a + b$ |
| `div` | `602 ÷ 7` | $a - b$ |

A misplaced point is the answer times or over 10. A slipped digit changes one digit by one, with no wrap from 9 to 0. Division must come out whole.
items.question: Write `battery_generator(seed, mix)`.

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests on fresh seeds. They check the count of each kind and every answer against its text. They check whole divisions, four different positive options with the answer once, and one near miss of each kind. One test uses 200 items; another checks that a seed repeats.

feedback.correct: Every item recomputes, and every distractor is one of the three near misses.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the failing row: it names the property that broke.

explain.text: Redrawing until the three near misses differ from each other and the answer is what keeps 200 items clean. A slipped 9 cannot wrap to 0, so it steps down instead. Section A of the full battery uses the same three near misses.

items.title: Answer or guess, in code
items.prose: A forward-only test at +1 and −1. `trade_values(seconds_needed, options_left, pace, accuracy, guess_seconds=2)` returns two exact averages over the same seconds. Both assume questions remain unreached when time ends, and the same accuracy on the slow question. Answering earns $2a - 1$. Guessing earns `guess_value(options_left)`, plus $\tfrac{s - g}{\text{pace}}$ questions at $2a - 1$ each. `answer_or_guess` returns `'guess'` only when guessing earns strictly more.
items.question: Complete `trade_values` and `answer_or_guess`.

widget.solution:
from fractions import Fraction


def guess_value(options_left, right=1, wrong=-1):
    k = options_left
    return Fraction(right) / k + Fraction(wrong) * (k - 1) / k


def trade_values(seconds_needed, options_left, pace, accuracy, guess_seconds=2):
    per_question = 2 * Fraction(accuracy) - 1
    answer = per_question
    guess = guess_value(options_left) + Fraction(seconds_needed - guess_seconds, pace) * per_question
    return answer, guess


def answer_or_guess(seconds_needed, options_left, pace, accuracy, guess_seconds=2):
    answer, guess = trade_values(seconds_needed, options_left, pace, accuracy, guess_seconds)
    return "guess" if guess > answer else "answer"
widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests, compared exactly. Four check pairs of averages as `Fraction`s; seven check decisions, two of them ties.

feedback.correct: Both functions match the lesson’s 0.8 against 2.4, and break ties towards answering.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every value a `Fraction`, and guess only on a strict win.

explain.text: At 50% accuracy every question is worth 0, so time buys nothing and a tie goes to answering. With two options left a guess is free, so a slow question nearly always becomes a guess. The 10 s case shows a blind guess among four is not worth a short saving.

items.title: One question, forward only
items.prose: A forward-only, negatively marked arithmetic question. Put the routine in order. Two lines are habits that cost marks: leave them out.
items.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Estimate the answer’s size before looking at the options
Remove the options your estimate rules out
Solve if it fits your pace; otherwise guess among what is left
Answer and move on, without looking back
Read the options first and pick the one that looks familiar
lines.why: Near-miss options are built to look familiar. Estimate first, then read them.

lines.text: Leave it unanswered and plan to come back at the end
lines.why: A forward-only test has no way back, and many do not allow a blank either.

feedback.correct: Read, estimate, remove, solve or guess, move on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The estimate comes before the options.

byKey.d1: Near-miss options are built to look familiar. Estimate first, then read them.
byKey.d2: A forward-only test has no way back, and many do not allow a blank either.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the two habits belongs.
byKey.s2: Estimate right after reading, before the options.
byKey.s3: Remove options once you have an estimate to test them against.
byKey.s4: Decide to solve or guess after removing what you can.
byKey.s5: Moving on is the last step.

explain.text: The estimate is what removes options, and removing two makes a guess free. Then solve or guess by the pace. Never plan to come back in a forward-only test.

items.title: Talk through your battery plan
items.prompt: Say your answer aloud first, for about 3 minutes, kept with your own watch; nothing is recorded. Then write it down and mark it against the rubric. The task: talk through your plan for a battery of arithmetic, sequences and probability, with negative marking on the arithmetic.
items.model:
**My plan for a battery: arithmetic with negative marking, then sequences, then probability.**

**Before it starts.** Five warm-up rounds in the morning, then a quiet room and a tested link. At the top of my paper I write the paces: arithmetic 6 s, sequences 100 s, probability 2 minutes.

**Arithmetic, +1 and −1, forward only.** Checkpoint Q10 at 1:00. For each question: read, estimate, remove options, then solve or guess. A blind guess averages −0.5, after removing one option $-\tfrac13$, after removing two 0. I answer when I am more than half sure. A 20 s question becomes a 2 s guess after removing two. The 18 s saved buys three questions at 0.8 each: 2.4 against 0.8.

**Sequences, no penalty.** About 100 s each: differences, ratios, split odd and even places, write each step, then digit rules. Never a blank: a guess earns a quarter-mark on average.

**Probability, no penalty.** About 2 minutes each, with the sample space or a crowd of 1,000 first. Fractions in lowest terms; anything above 1 or below 0 goes at once. I do not carry arithmetic speed in here.

**Habits.** In the first minute of each section I settle into its pace instead of racing. One breath between sections. If I finish a section early, I recheck only its flagged items.

**Afterwards.** Net score per section, then slips, method gaps and time losses against each section’s pace. One drill for next week.

rubric.text: Gives each section’s pace (6 s, 100 s, 2 minutes) and at least one checkpoint or switch time.
States the negative-marking values: −0.5 blind, −1/3 after one removal, 0 after two, and answering when more than half sure.
Never leaves a blank where a wrong answer costs nothing.
Explains the time trade on a slow question, with numbers.
Applies the first-minute rule, a breath between sections, and a fresh pace for each section.
Names a method for each section: estimate and last digit; the sequence tests in order; sample space first.
Uses spare time only on flagged items in the open section.
Spoke for about 3 minutes, in order, without reading a script.
